“Did you see the banner come down?” Sahil laughed, then stopped. “I ripped it, Pranav. Me.”

“I saw,” Pranav said. “Dev was cheering you on.”

“Everyone was chanting. The whole stand felt like one big body. I'd never tear something of someone else's if I was alone.”

“You went at it like you were angry.”

“I wasn't angry. That's the odd part. I just stopped being me for a minute.”

Dev jogged up. “Come on, food! That was a legend moment.”

Pranav shook his head. “Not for the kid who made that banner, Dev. It was his whole week.”

Sahil looked at his hands. “I'll find their group and offer to pay for the cloth.”

“I'll come,” Pranav said.

qa.q: Who was cheering Sahil on?
qa.a: Dev was cheering Sahil on.

qa.q: What did Sahil mean by saying, “I just stopped being me for a minute”?
qa.a: Sahil meant that inside the chanting crowd Sahil felt bolder and less accountable, and did something never done alone.

qa.q: What choice did Sahil make after looking at both hands?
qa.a: Sahil decided to find the other group and offer to pay for the cloth.

qa.q: How might the person who made the banner feel about a whole week of work being torn down?
qa.a: The banner maker probably felt hurt and angry, and powerless against a crowd that treated it as fun.

grounding: A young adult at a match feels bolder and less accountable in the crowd and tears a banner he would never touch alone.

passage:
I'm Omkar, and last winter at the college fest I learned something about myself. The last act was over and the crowd rushed the gate to the backstage lane. Ankita, my friend from the dance club, caught my sleeve and said, “Don't.” I went anyway. Hundreds of us pushed at the steel barricade, and someone shouted to lift it. I put both hands on it and heaved. The guard's face was frightened. Alone in a quiet hallway I would never have done that. In the crowd my courage felt huge and nobody's fault, least of all mine.

On the walk home Ankita said nothing. Finally I said, “That wasn't me.” Ankita answered, “It was you, though.” I've been thinking about that ever since.

qa.q: What did Ankita say when catching Omkar's sleeve?
qa.a: Ankita caught Omkar's sleeve and said, “Don't.”

qa.q: Why did Omkar's courage feel like nobody's fault, least of all Omkar's?
qa.a: In the crowd Omkar felt bold and hidden among hundreds, so responsibility seemed to spread out until it almost disappeared.

qa.q: What could Omkar try the next time a crowd starts pushing at a barricade?
qa.a: Omkar could listen to a friend's warning like Ankita's and step out of the surge before touching the barricade.

qa.q: What might the guard have felt while the crowd heaved at the barricade?
qa.a: The guard was probably frightened and outnumbered, worried about being hurt or unable to control the crowd.

grounding: A young adult at a fest feels bolder and less accountable in a crowd and does something never done alone.

passage:
Dear Maria,
You asked about the fee protest. It was the strangest day.
There were maybe two thousand of us outside the admin block. I'm shy, you know that. But in that crowd, with everyone chanting, I climbed on a bench and shouted the slogans louder than anyone. I felt fearless. For once I wasn't scared of anyone looking at me.
And then, when the gate didn't open, some boys kicked the flowerpots along the path. I kicked one too. Just like that. I'd never do that alone, not in a hundred years. The gardener, old Ramdas kaka, was standing right there.
I went back the next morning to help him replant them. He didn't say anything. I felt like two different people.
Sarita

qa.q: How many people were outside the admin block?
qa.a: Maybe two thousand.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel standing on the bench?
qa.a: Sarita felt fearless and bold, free for once from worrying about people looking.

qa.q: What did Sarita do to repair the damage, and why was it right?
qa.a: Sarita went back to help Ramdas kaka replant the flowerpots, taking personal responsibility for what the crowd did.

qa.q: How might Ramdas kaka have felt watching the flowerpots kicked?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and sad, seeing his work destroyed by students he looked after.

grounding: A young woman writes about feeling bolder in a protest crowd, which freed courage but also led to damaging property the writer never would alone.

passage:
Okay, you want the stadium story? I'm Deepika, and I'm not proud of this one.
It was the big final. Me, Arnab and forty thousand people. Our team was losing, and our whole stand started booing the other side's fans. At home I don't even raise my voice. But there, I booed so loud my throat hurt. It felt great. Like I was taller.
Then some guys near us started throwing paper cups at a family in the other team's shirts. And I threw mine. I don't even remember deciding.
The little boy in that family ducked behind his father. Arnab grabbed my arm. “Deepika, what are you doing?”
I sat down. I felt sick. I'd never do that on my own. Never.

qa.q: How many people were at the stadium?
qa.a: Forty thousand people.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel after throwing the cup?
qa.a: Deepika felt sick and ashamed, realising it was something never done alone.

qa.q: What does Arnab's reaction show about stepping in?
qa.a: A friend grabbing an arm and asking a direct question can break the crowd's spell and bring someone back to themselves.

qa.q: How might the little boy in the family have felt?
qa.a: He was probably frightened, ducking behind his father as cups flew at them.

grounding: A young adult recalls feeling bolder in a stadium crowd, which led to throwing a cup at a family, something never done alone.

passage:
The day before Holi: Mahima told Gurpreet she'd stay on the terrace. Crowds made her nervous.
Holi: By noon, the whole lane was a sea of colour and drums. Mahima went down just to watch, and in minutes she was in the middle, laughing, throwing colour at everyone, grabbing water balloons. She felt light, wild, invisible. When an old man with a walking stick shook his head, “No colour, please,” she laughed and threw a handful at him anyway. The crowd cheered.
The day after: Mahima saw the same man outside the chemist, scrubbing pink from his white kurta, his hands trembling. She stopped. Gurpreet said, “Isn't that—” Mahima nodded. She walked over and said, “Uncle, I'm sorry. That was me.”

qa.q: What did the old man say to Mahima?
qa.a: He said, "No colour, please."

qa.q: How did Mahima feel in the Holi crowd?
qa.a: She felt light, wild and invisible, bolder than she ever felt alone.

qa.q: What did Mahima do the day after, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She went to the old man and apologised, taking personal responsibility for what she did in the crowd.

qa.q: How might the old man have felt when colour was thrown at him?
qa.a: He probably felt disrespected and upset, having clearly asked for no colour.

grounding: Shows a young woman who feels bolder and less accountable in a festival crowd and does something she never would alone.

Afreen, you asked if I ever did anything wild in college. Sit. Your Tanuja mausi was twenty, at the inter-college football final in Kolkata.
Forty thousand people, and I was never a loud girl. But that night, deep in the crowd, I sang, I screamed, I stood on my seat. I felt ten feet tall. Nobody knew me; nobody was watching. That part was wonderful.
Then our team lost, and the people near us started throwing bottles at the other side's stand. I picked up an empty one. My arm was already back. I would never, ever have done that alone.
My friend Rumi caught my wrist. "Tanu. That's not you." I dropped it, and my knees went weak. We left by the back gate before the police came in.
Being one of many gave me my voice that night, Afreen. It nearly gave me something much worse too.

qa.q: How many people were in the stadium?
qa.a: Forty thousand people.

qa.q: How did young Tanuja feel standing on the seat and singing?
qa.a: She felt bold and free, "ten feet tall", because nobody in the huge crowd knew her or was watching.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Rumi catching her wrist and saying "That's not you"; one friend reminded her who she was before the crowd decided for her.

qa.q: What might Rumi have felt catching Tanuja's wrist?
qa.a: Rumi was probably alarmed but steady, sure enough of who Tanuja really was to step in.

grounding: Shows a young adult at a match feeling bolder and less accountable in the crowd, which frees her voice but almost leads to an act she would never do alone.
